drills.q: Is Azure Synapse Analytics deprecated? State Microsoft's actual current guidance precisely.
drills.a: Not deprecated -- maintenance mode: security/reliability patches continue, no major new capability investment. All new engineering (Copilot, Direct Lake, OneLake, Data Agents, Spark 4.0) goes to Fabric. Guidance: new work starts on Fabric, existing Synapse workloads keep running, migration is phased over months to years, not a forced cutover.

drills.q: Explain OneLake and why it's the real architectural differentiator between Fabric and Synapse, not just a UI change.
drills.a: OneLake is one logical, tenant-wide Delta Parquet data lake that every Fabric workload (Lakehouse, Warehouse, Power BI Direct Lake, Real-Time Intelligence) reads/writes directly with zero cross-engine duplication. Synapse's separate pools (Dedicated SQL, Serverless SQL, Spark) typically require actual data movement between them to combine, which OneLake eliminates by design.

drills.q: A Fabric capacity shows slow Power BI reports and late pipeline completions around the same time. Diagnose.
drills.a: Fabric's throttling is a smoothing algorithm, not a hard cutoff: sustained usage above CU capacity delays background operations (pipelines) first, escalating to interactive-operation throttling (live reports) only if overage persists. Both symptoms are likely the same root cause -- capacity pressure -- diagnosed by checking CU utilization trend rather than treating them as separate incidents.

drills.q: What documented utilization signals indicate a Fabric F-SKU upgrade is needed rather than just continued monitoring?
drills.a: Average CU utilization sustained above 75% for 2+ weeks, more than one throttling event per week at the same time of day, or peak-hour utilization sustained above 150%. Reactive one-off spikes don't necessarily require an upgrade; sustained patterns matching these signals do.

drills.q: Compare how Azure Data Factory and Fabric Data Factory are billed, and the capacity-planning implication.
drills.a: ADF is standalone, separately provisioned/billed (activity runs, ~$0.274/vCore-hr data flow, IR hours). Fabric Data Factory draws from the Fabric capacity's shared CU pool alongside every other workload -- effectively free against existing CU spend, but heavy/spiky ETL now competes for the same capacity as latency-sensitive workloads like Power BI refreshes, a contention risk standalone ADF never had.

drills.q: Explain Event Hubs' Kafka-compatible endpoint and one concrete limitation to verify before migrating a Kafka application.
drills.a: It's a protocol-compatibility layer -- existing Kafka producer/consumer code points at it via bootstrap-server and SASL/OAuth config changes only, no app rewrite for standard produce/consume. Limitation: some Kafka-specific admin APIs and exactly-once transactional semantics guarantees lack full parity with a real Kafka broker -- verify specific dependencies before committing to migration.

drills.q: State Event Hubs Standard tier's real throughput numbers and what happens when a producer exceeds them.
drills.a: 1 Throughput Unit = up to 1MB/s or 1,000 events/s ingress (whichever hits first), up to 2MB/s or 4,096 events/s egress. Self-serve cap 20 TUs (40 via support ticket). Standard tier hard-throttles at the provisioned ceiling with throttling errors, not graceful degradation -- requires proactive TU scaling ahead of known traffic spikes.

drills.q: A workload needs the highest, most predictable sustained Event Hubs throughput on dedicated infrastructure. Which tier and minimum commitment?
drills.a: Dedicated tier, billed in Capacity Units, minimum deployment of 8 CUs -- single-tenant dedicated infrastructure. Scaling beyond 10 CUs requires a support request. Unlike Standard, it's capacity-based (not hard-throttled), matching Premium's model but with dedicated infra.

drills.q: Compare Synapse Dedicated SQL Pool billing to Serverless SQL Pool billing and explain when each wins.
drills.a: Dedicated SQL Pool is cluster-billed per DWU-hour regardless of query volume -- wins for predictable, sustained, high-concurrency workloads. Serverless SQL Pool is billed per TB scanned, query-in-place with no provisioned cluster -- wins for sporadic, exploratory, low-frequency query patterns where idle provisioned capacity would waste money.

drills.q: Design a migration plan for a company with a stable Synapse Dedicated Pool warehouse and a growing need for near-real-time Power BI dashboards.
drills.a: Keep the stable Synapse warehouse running -- no urgent migration driver for a functioning workload. Provision new Fabric capacity specifically for the near-real-time dashboard need, using OneLake and Direct Lake mode to give Power BI fresh data without a separate import/refresh cycle -- exactly the capability Fabric was built for and Synapse wasn't. Migrate the Synapse warehouse later only if a concrete new-capability need or maintenance-mode risk materializes.

drills.q: Explain why cluster-billed warehouses and scan-billed query-in-place systems represent fundamentally different cost-modeling disciplines.
drills.a: Cluster-billed (Dedicated Pool, Redshift) requires capacity planning ahead of load; cost is roughly fixed whether the cluster is idle or fully loaded. Scan-billed (Serverless SQL Pool, BigQuery) shifts the discipline to controlling how much data each query scans -- partitioning and query design directly reduce cost, with no idle-capacity waste but real risk of cost surprise from an unexpectedly expensive ad-hoc query. Neither is universally cheaper; it depends on usage pattern.
